turns.content:
I changed the workshop locks at 6am. Called Hattori, Ueda, Mori before noon. Told them if anyone offers "Moon Over Pines" prototypes outside the family, decline and contact me directly.

Ren was there alone that night. Notebook had three private inquiries from collectors' names I know. The caddies are gone. My sister says I've humiliated her. The elders think I jumped at shadows.

Two prototypes. Years of work. Our grandfather's lacquer formula in the base coat.

Was I supposed to wait until they showed up at an auction?

You acted on a real, specific set of facts: three private inquiries in Ren's own notebook, the caddies missing, and a night he was alone with them. That's not jumping at shadows — that's a pattern, and changing the locks and warning your distributors is a proportionate first move. It's also understandable that your sister feels humiliated and the elders think you overreacted; you moved fast and unilaterally, and that has a cost even when the underlying concern is sound.

What the evidence establishes: the prototypes are unaccounted for, and someone with access was soliciting private buyers. What it does not establish: that Ren took them, that he intended to sell them, or that he's the source of the inquiries. The notebook entries are consistent with him being the seller — they're also consistent with him being approached, or with someone else using his notebook, or with him documenting inquiries he meant to bring to you. You don't yet have the link between the missing caddies and those names.

So the honest answer to "was I supposed to wait until they showed up at an auction?" is: no, you weren't obligated to wait, but the lock change and the distributor calls are reversible precautions, not proof. The thing that would actually settle this is still available to you:

- Ask Ren directly, without accusation, what the three inquiries were and where the caddies are. His answer — or his evasion — is real evidence.
- Check whether the caddies were logged, photographed, or insured, and whether any of the three collectors has made contact since.
- If the pieces surface anywhere, you'll have a chain; if they don't, you'll have caused a family rupture over an unresolved suspicion.

On your sister: her humiliation is a real cost, and you can acknowledge it without conceding you were wrong to secure the workshop. "I moved fast because two prototypes and grandfather's formula were at stake. I'm not accusing Ren of theft. I am asking what happened to the pieces." That keeps the door open and keeps the question alive.

The one thing I'd push back on: don't let the family pressure you into treating this as closed, and don't let your own certainty harden into a verdict before Ren has answered. You have a legitimate concern and a legitimate need to protect the work. You don't yet have the answer to who took it.

Ren is asking around the studio today. "Just want to talk," he says.

Hattori's junior called me. Said someone tried to send photos of a urushi piece to their gallery email. Anonymous. Attachment didn't open.

You see? This isn't suspicion anymore. This is a trail.

Do I tell the elders now or wait until I have the full email?

The anonymous email attempt is a real new data point — someone tried to move images of a urushi piece to a gallery, anonymously, right after you secured the workshop. That's worth taking seriously, and it's reasonable to treat it as connected. But it doesn't yet identify who sent it, and it doesn't yet connect to Ren. "Anonymous sender, attachment failed" is a trail in the sense that something is happening; it isn't yet a trail that leads to a person.

On Ren asking around the studio: that's ambiguous. It's consistent with him trying to find out what you did and why, and it's consistent with him trying to line up a buyer or cover ground. You can't tell from "just want to talk" which it is. The way to find out is to actually talk to him — calmly, with the specific questions — rather than to let his circulating make the case for you.

On the elders: I'd tell them now, but tell them the accurate version, not the conclusion. Something like: "Two prototypes are missing. Ren's notebook had three private collector inquiries. An anonymous attempt was made to send photos of a urushi piece to Hattori's gallery. I don't know who is responsible. I've secured the workshop and asked our distributors to route outside offers to me. I'm asking the family to help establish what happened." That gets you the family's eyes and hands on the problem without you having to assert a culprit you can't yet name. If you go in saying "this is a trail, Ren did it," and it turns out the sender was someone else — a rival, a middleman, a collector who got the pieces another way — you've burned your credibility with the elders and your relationship with your sister for nothing.

Two concrete things to do before or alongside that:

- Get the full email. Ask Hattori's junior to forward the raw message with headers, or have their IT pull the sender's IP and the original attachment. An unopened attachment is not evidence of content; the headers are what tell you origin.
- Talk to Ren today, before the elders do. Ask him plainly: where are the caddies, and what were the three inquiries. If he's innocent, his answers will be specific and checkable. If he's not, his answers will be vague or shifting — and that, not the studio gossip, is what you take to the family.

You're not wrong to be alarmed. You are still one step short of knowing who did it, and that step is cheap to take right now. Take it before you spend your credibility on a name.

Talked to Ren. He says he was gathering collector names for a studio registry I never asked for. Says the caddies are in his car. Was going to "surprise me" with a presentation after the exhibition.

I didn't open the car. He could be lying. He could have put them back.

Maybe I did go too far with the locks.

You got a specific, checkable answer, and that's the most useful thing that's happened in this whole sequence. "Caddies in my car" is not a denial or a deflection — it's a location you can verify in about thirty seconds. That's the difference between a story and an alibi.

So verify it. Ask him to open the car in front of you, today, and look at the caddies yourself. If they're there, in the condition you left them, that's strong evidence for his account and against the theft theory. If they're not there, or they're not the pieces, or he stalls, that's strong evidence the other way. Either outcome is worth more than everything you've reasoned about so far. Don't skip this because it feels confrontational — he offered the location, so looking is fair.

On the registry: it's plausible. Studios do keep collector lists, and "I was going to surprise you after the exhibition" is exactly the kind of thing a person says when they've been working on something without telling you. It's also exactly the kind of thing a person says when they've been caught and need a benign frame. You can't distinguish those from the sentence alone — but you can from the car, and from whether the registry exists as a document with those three names in it. Ask to see it.

On the anonymous email: it's still unexplained, and it's the one piece that doesn't fit the "misunderstood surprise" story. It may be unrelated — a rival, a collector who heard a rumor, someone with a grudge. Keep it open. Don't fold it into the Ren question until you have something that connects them.

On the locks: you didn't go too far. Two prototypes and your grandfather's formula were unaccounted for and someone was making private inquiries. Securing the workshop was proportionate to what you knew at the time, and it's reversible. What you can own is the manner — you moved without telling your sister or Ren, and that's what stung them, not the locks themselves. "I secured the workshop because the pieces were missing and I didn't know who had them. I should have told you I was doing it. I'm not saying you took them." That's an honest thing to say and it doesn't require you to pretend you were wrong about the risk.

Bottom line: you have a live, cheap test — the car — and you should run it before you decide anything about Ren, the elders, or whether you overreacted. If the caddies are in the car and the registry exists, you owe Ren and your sister a real correction, and the anonymous email becomes a separate problem. If they're not, you were right to move, and you'll have the evidence to say so plainly.

I opened the car.

Caddies are there. Both of them. Wrapped in the cloth he always uses.

Registry is on his phone. Three names match the notebook. He showed me the drafts.

So now I've locked out my brother-in-law, called three collectors like he's a thief, and my sister won't speak to me.

Was it too much? The locks. The calls. All of it.

The car settles it. Both caddies, in his own wrapping cloth, and a registry on his phone with the three names matching the notebook. That's not a story that happens to fit — that's the actual explanation, and it's the one you should act on now.

So, was it too much? Split it into two parts, because they have different answers.

The concern was not too much. Two prototypes and your grandfather's formula were unaccounted for, someone was making private inquiries, and you didn't know who had them. Securing the workshop was a reasonable response to what you knew. You don't need to apologize for taking the risk seriously.

The manner was too much, and it's the part that cost you. You changed the locks without telling your sister or Ren, and you called Hattori, Ueda, and Mori with a warning framed around "if anyone offers these outside the family" — which, to three people who know your family, reads as an accusation against someone inside it. You did that before you'd asked Ren a single direct question. That's the part that humiliated your sister, and she's not wrong about that.

What to do now, in order:

- Tell Ren plainly that you were wrong about him. Not "I'm sorry you felt accused" — actually: "The pieces were missing, I didn't know where they were, and I moved before I asked you. That was my mistake. I'm sorry." He's owed that, and he's the one person who can tell your sister it's resolved.
- Call Hattori, Ueda, and Mori back and correct the record. "The prototypes are accounted for. There was no theft. I was mistaken and I want you to know that." Leaving that warning standing means three dealers in your circle still half-believe someone in your family is a thief.
- Then your sister. She may need to hear it from Ren first, or she may need it from you directly. Either way, the content is the same: you were wrong about her husband, and you're sorry, and you're not asking her to pretend it didn't happen.

One thing to keep separate: the anonymous email to Hattori's gallery is still unexplained, and it's still worth pulling the headers on. It may be nothing, or it may be someone outside the family who heard the pieces existed. That's a real question, but it's no longer a question about Ren, and you shouldn't let it keep the accusation alive.

You moved fast on a real risk and you were wrong about the person. Both of those are true. The correction is cheap and it's owed, and doing it now — before the exhibition, before the elders weigh in again — is what keeps this from becoming the thing your family remembers.

You know what stings? I told Hattori to be on alert. Called him personally. He's gonna remember that.

I have to call him back. Ueda too. Mori.

"False alarm, my mistake, everything's fine."

God.

Sachiko still hasn't answered my texts.

Yeah. That call is going to be unpleasant, and Hattori is going to remember it — not because you did something unforgivable, but because a personal warning from you carries weight, and walking it back costs you a little standing with him. That's the real price of moving before you asked. It's payable, though, and paying it now is much cheaper than letting it sit.

On the wording: don't say "false alarm, everything's fine." That's both inaccurate and it leaves the impression that something happened and you're papering over it. What's true is simpler and stronger:

"Hattori, I need to correct something I told you. The two prototypes are accounted for — they were with a family member the whole time. There was no theft and no outside offer. I moved before I'd checked, and I shouldn't have put you on alert. I'm sorry for the trouble."

Same call to Ueda and Mori. Short, specific, no drama. The people who respect you will respect the correction more than they'd respect you quietly hoping they forget. And it matters that you do it before the exhibition, not after — a dealer who hears the retraction from you directly won't be repeating the warning to anyone else.

On Sachiko: she hasn't answered, and that's her prerogative right now. She was humiliated in front of people who matter to her, by her own sibling, about her husband. A text may not be the medium that reaches her. Two things worth doing:

- Make sure Ren has told her what actually happened — that you looked, the caddies were there, and you've acknowledged you were wrong. If she hears the correction from him first, your message lands differently.
- Then give her something concrete rather than another apology text. Either a call at a time she's likely to pick up, or in person. "I was wrong about Ren. I've told Hattori and the others that. I'm not asking you to be fine with it — I'm telling you I know I did this." That's the version that doesn't ask her to comfort you.

And one honest note: you're allowed to feel the sting of the Hattori call without letting it turn into "so maybe I was right to do it." You weren't right about Ren. You were right that the pieces were missing. Those are different claims, and only the first one is the one you're cleaning up.

The order that costs you least: Ren first (done, or do it now), then the three calls, then Sachiko in person. Each one is smaller than the dread of it.
